The objective of offline reinforcement learning is to develop policies based on fixed datasets without any subsequent online interactions. This challenge is particularly demanding due to its inherent complexity. Existing methods, such as V-Learning and FQI, are incomplete, necessitating additional interactions for accurate policy evaluation, whereas popular benchmark FKI is inefficient, requiring a large number of iterations. This paper presents a novel offline reinforcement learning approach called Limited Sample Examination of Minimax (LSEM), which offers several key improvements. Firstly, it addresses the incompleteness issue by achieving lower sample complexity compared to existing methods. Secondly, it significantly reduces the number of iterations needed, outperforming FKI in this regard. Furthermore, LSEM is the first offline reinforcement learning approach to achieve an optimal first-order convergence rate, solidifying its position as a leading solution in this field. Additionally, we have developed an improved version of LSEM, called Limited Sample Examination of Minimax with Projection (LSEM-P), which offers enhanced robustness in real-world applications. Our theoretical findings are supported by extensive simulations, which demonstrate the superiority of LSEM and LSEM-P over existing methods in various scenarios. Recent breakthroughs in neural abstractive summarization models have shown
substantial improvement over traditional methods. However, a major concern remains
with these models producing summaries that deviate significantly from actual source
text content. Research has demonstrated that incorporating source information can
mitigate this issue. Nevertheless, a more effective solution involves teaching the
model to adhere to the source's factual accuracy without sacrificing overall summary
comprehension. This study presents a novel approach to address this challenge by
leveraging a unique training signal that combines source text and summary facts.
The proposed signal is obtained through a novel abstractive summarization model
capable of extracting relevant facts from the source text. The results of our experiments
on various summarization benchmarks demonstrate that this novel approach yields
more accurate summaries that retain the essence of the source text. Specifically, we
achieve notable improvements in factuality and fluency on the CNN and MediaNLP
datasets. The proposed method also excels in low-resource settings and outperforms
leading baselines in terms of factuality and fluency. The accompanying code and
evaluation scripts are publicly available for further research and development.

Cache side-channel attacks have been identified as a threat to software security, 
allowing attackers to extract sensitive information by analyzing cache collisions. 
While recent research has developed methods to detect and mitigate these attacks, 
a key challenge remains in understanding the underlying causes of cache side-channel vulnerabilities. 

To address this challenge, we introduce CacheQL, a novel tool for measuring 
cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software. CacheQL leverages a unique 
approach that combines a cache-unsafe programming model with a robust profiling 
and monitoring system to accurately quantify cache side-channel weaknesses in 
affected applications. 

We demonstrate the effectiveness of CacheQL in assessing the cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in popular third-party libraries, specifically in QEMU, Nettle, and 
LibGCompr. Our results show that QEMU and Nettle suffer from cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities, while LibGCompr has significant vulnerabilities in its CPU and 
memory access components. 

We also propose a method to localize the root causes of cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in software, which we demonstrate in our analysis of LibGCompr, 
identifying a specific instruction set and cache line combination that causes 
vulnerabilities. 

Our research highlights the practical value of CacheQL in assessing cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in production software, providing a new tool for developers and 
security auditors to accurately measure and localize these threats. 

We make CacheQL source code publicly available for research and development 
purposes, and invite researchers to contribute to its development. 

Our study also reveals that while existing software mitigations, such as cache 
bypassing and randomization, can reduce cache side-channel attacks, they do not 
eliminate the underlying vulnerabilities. 

Our research findings suggest that a combination of software design and development 
practices is necessary to prevent and detect cache side-channel attacks. 

We make a call to action for software developers and security auditors to adopt 
this research and work together to address the cache side-channel threat, 
providing a more secure and reliable software stack for the future. 

Our research findings and the CacheQL tool are available at 
https://github.com/UCeFT/CacheQL. 

We also present our research at the USENIX Security 2021 conference.

Specifically, we analyze the behavior of our solvers in the context of regularized SV formulations for linear parabolic optimal control problems. The proposed solvers are implemented within the PETSc framework, which allows for seamless parallelization and high performance. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide an open-source implementation of our solvers on GitHub. To address the issue of mode collapse in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), researchers have proposed various methods such as adding noise to the input, using multiple generators, and incorporating auxiliary classification tasks. These approaches have been examined in existing studies, yet there remains a need to understand how changes in the GAN loss affect the presence of modes. This paper presents an empirical analysis of four methods to prevent mode collapse, focusing on the impact of changes in the Hessian eigenvalues of the GAN loss function. Specifically, the Hessian matrix is crucial in determining the GAN loss landscape and its eigenvalues indicate the presence of local minima. Our experiments reveal that the modes associated with positive eigenvalues can be recovered through a process known as mode retrieval. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mode retrieval method outperforms existing approaches in mode regularization and provide additional insights into the effectiveness of the Laplacian and gradient penalty methods. Our findings also highlight the limitations of the mode retrieval method and suggest avenues for future research. Ultimately, this study aims to advance the field of GANs and inspire the development of more robust mode regularization techniques. Researchers have developed predictive models for analyzing the intricate interactions between different layers of these networks. This suggests that future advancements in multilayer network predictive models will draw heavily from the successes achieved in single-layer graph algorithms. This finding highlights the potential of the algorithm to improve predictive capabilities in environments where data collection is challenging. Overall, our research indicates that GraphSAGE-based approaches can be effectively adapted for use in multilayer networks, and that they hold great promise for predicting interactions between different layers of complex, interconnected systems. CLIP, a state-of-the-art large-scale model, has achieved significant success in
image-text matching by leveraging both human and machine annotations. However,
this model's performance is limited by its lack of adaptability to new and
unseen environments, which is a major concern in practical applications. To
overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel method called Domain Prompt
Learning (DPL), which enables CLIP to perform well in areas it has never
encountered before. DPL involves generating effective prompts using a
domain-specific dataset, which are then combined with CLIP to form a
modified architecture called CLIP+Prompt. Notably, CLIP+Prompt does not
require any fine-tuning process, and it can even outperform the original CLIP
model. To further improve performance, we also propose a Prompt Fine-tuning
module, which is designed to adjust the prompts generated by DPL to better
align with the specific requirements of downstream tasks. By integrating this
module with DPL, we have developed a comprehensive framework that can handle
domain shift and supports end-to-end fine-tuning. When applied to a variety
of downstream tasks, our approach consistently delivers superior results,
demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness. The code for DPL is available
for public access at https://github.com/Leakylion/Domain-Prompt-For-CLIP. We
hope that our research will drive the development of more versatile and
adaptable vision-language models in the future. The associated code can be
found at https://github.com/Leakylion/Domain-Prompt-For-CLIP. Additional
supplementary materials are available at https://leakylion.github.io/DPL. The
authors would be delighted to hear from anyone interested in extending this work.

The quality of dehazed images often relies heavily on the subjective perception of observers. This paper introduces innovative 3D object localization techniques by proposing two distinct array coding strategies. These coded assessment protocols utilize passive backscatter communication from the target, incorporating a sequence of modulated signals transmitted by a reference device. The sequence encodes three-dimensional coordinates, which are decoded by analyzing the phase shifts of the reflected signals at multiple discrete angles. To enhance coding efficiency, we developed two protocols: the Sphere Array Coding (SAC) and the Sphere Array Coding with Rotation (SCAR). Our analysis demonstrates that scalable coding techniques allow for precise 3D localization of a target object, and we provide mathematical expressions for the positioning error of our coding schemes. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we explore the impact of practical implementation factors, such as noise, antenna array size, and reference device transmission power on the performance of our coding strategies. Our results show that the SCAR protocol significantly outperforms the SAC in scenarios with limited antenna resources, and we believe that our findings have the potential to revolutionize the field of three-dimensional object localization. A new pre-mature termination criterion for the GMRES algorithm used in the IP method to solve symmetric positive definite linear systems is proposed. This criterion relies on the relationship between early termination and the residual norm being less than the product of the smallest and largest eigenvalue of the system's matrix multiplied by the norm of the error. By computing this product at the initial step, the need for recurrent computation during Krylov methods is avoided. A comparison with a widely used, but unstable, termination criterion based on residual growth is shown through numerical experiments, demonstrating the new criterion's stability and potential to reduce computational costs. Additionally, the potential for early termination of other Krylov methods, such as GMRES, CG, and MINRES, is explored. However, results indicate that while early termination is possible, it is not consistently more beneficial than using GMRES with the proposed termination criterion. This is likely due to GMRES's ability to provide accurate results in subsequent IP method iterations. As a result, our proposed termination criterion is recommended for implementation within Krylov methods. In ensemble Q-learning, combining multiple value functions can lead to a significant improvement in performance over individual methods. Specifically, a measure of value function diversity must be used to ensure that the value functions are diverse, but not excessively so, as this can lead to a deterioration of the value function estimates. We propose a novel algorithm, SVFD, which optimizes representation diversity by using this measure, and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods on various benchmark tasks. Our results show that SVFD not only outperforms individual methods, but also surpasses other ensemble Q-learning techniques in performance and sample efficiency. We also show that SVFD can effectively handle non-stationary environments and improve performance in these situations. Ultimately, our work reveals the importance of carefully managing representation diversity to achieve the full benefits of ensemble Q-learning. In the field of multi-task learning, there is a common approach where multiple tasks are forecasted simultaneously using a shared model. However, this approach faces challenges when tasks are highly correlated, resulting in "concept contamination" where the model learns unrelated information, reducing the accuracy of task forecasts. To address this issue, we propose a new method called Joint Predictability Enhancer (JPE), which enhances the accuracy of task forecasts by improving the precision of multi-task predictions. JPE does this by predicting task correlations and then combining forecast vectors in a way that reduces the impact of irrelevant information. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in a series of experiments involving diverse and challenging tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is particularly effective in highly correlated task settings, where others fall short. Overall, our method provides a practical solution for enhancing the accuracy of task forecasts in multi-task learning scenarios. Code for our method is available for public use on GitHub.

A novel approach to attribute extraction in time series involves a two-part process: first, identify and isolate a subset of relevant features, and then compute their values. This paper introduces a dynamic filter based on the variance of the feature values over time, which selectively focuses on only the most dynamic characteristics, reducing complexity and computational demands while maintaining performance. The dynamic filter's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in both a basic and an ensemble setting, yielding results that surpass those achieved by state-of-the-art methods in the field of multi-fault diagnosis for industrial bearings. The ensemble model, in particular, exhibits superior performance, with significant improvements in accuracy, precision, and F1-measure when compared to the most basic competitor. The proposed dynamic filter's ability to selectively focus on only the most dynamic characteristics allows for a substantial reduction in computational demands, from approximately 1.9 million operations per sample and model down to around 8,400 operations per sample and model. The accompanying source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexsqz/Filter-Based-Attribute-Extraction. A new inverse problem addresses the relationship between the levels of RNA polymerase II in a cell and the corresponding changes in mRNA concentrations over time. This problem is significant in systems biology because understanding the dynamics of mRNAs is crucial for studying gene expression. Current methods for measuring RNA levels are based on immunocapture and quantitative PCR but these techniques have their limitations. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a novel approach that uses a mechanistic model to predict mRNA levels based on time-series data. This approach involves solving a system of ordinary differential equations that describe the relationship between RNA polymerase II levels and mRNA transcription. We have successfully applied this approach to a study of human breast cancer cells undergoing treatment with a combination of chemotherapies. Our results show that the proposed model accurately predicts the dynamics of mRNAs and identifies the regulatory mechanisms controlling them. Furthermore, we have used this model to simulate the effects of different treatment regimens and evaluated their effectiveness. Our findings suggest that the model can be used to predict the effects of various treatments and identify the optimal treatment strategies. This approach has the potential to be applied to a wide range of applications in systems biology, enabling the prediction of mRNA levels and the identification of regulatory elements. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and accuracy of this approach, paving the way for its application in the analysis of human cancer cells and other biological systems. This study presents an innovative, user-friendly visual approach to categorize and interpret multi-dimensional data. Our goal is to create a method that maintains a delicate equilibrium between the effectiveness of data grouping and the clarity of data representation. Our analysis reveals a direct relationship between the variety of data attributes and the ideal number of data groups, and we propose a novel, data-driven method for automatically determining this number. Our approach is evaluated using multiple real-world datasets, and we compare its results to those of prominent data visualization techniques. Our findings demonstrate that well-designed, minimal visualizations can effectively convey meaningful insights and facilitate understanding, even with large multi-dimensional data sets. These visualizations also enable effective analysis and interpretation of data grouping patterns. Ultimately, we discuss the implications of our work, highlighting its potential to enhance the effectiveness of data-driven discovery and decision-making through data visualization. The spread of false information on social media is a pressing issue that requires immediate attention. In response, social media platforms have implemented countermeasures such as flagging suspicious content and removing it. However, these efforts are hindered by the creation of fake content designed to evade detection. To address this issue, we propose a method for generating training data that can help differentiate between genuine and false news on social media. Our approach relies on the presence of propaganda in false content, which is characterized by its style and structure. To create a dataset that captures this propaganda, we developed a content generator that uses a transformer-based model to create false content mirroring genuine content in terms of structure and style. Using this generator, we collected a dataset of 1000 false news articles and 1000 genuine articles. Our analysis of the generated content indicates that it effectively replicates the style and structure of propaganda found in false content, while maintaining a high level of coherence. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a case study on detecting false content related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Our results show that fine-tuning BERT on our generated data leads to improved false content detection, outperforming a baseline model by 5.5% in F1 score. Moreover, we found that our generated content is more similar to false content than genuine content, indicating that it can help identify false content in real-world scenarios. Our research contributes to the field of false content detection by introducing a content generator that can help identify propaganda-filled content. The integration of HVDC links into power systems has significant implications for their operation and control, particularly when it comes to maintaining frequency stability. As these links become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to understand their impact on system behavior. This research focuses on identifying the relationship between HVDC power flow and frequency stability using explainable AI, specifically by applying partial dependence plots to data from the Nordic power system. The results show that HVDC power can be expressed as a function of system conditions, indicating that specific variables have a greater influence on their operation. Furthermore, it is found that HVDC activation can lead to reduced complexity in frequency stability analysis, yet it also increases the likelihood of instability if not considered in stability assessments. The findings of this study are validated through detailed simulations involving various system disturbances. The methodology employed in this research is versatile and can be applied to other power systems, enabling a deeper understanding of the connections between HVDC power flow and frequency stability. This understanding is crucial for the effective operation of future power systems that rely heavily on HVDC links. This paper introduces a novel adversarial training method tailored to tabular data and the challenges associated with imbalanced training datasets. We propose the Antagonistic Assault Training (AAT) method, which simultaneously trains two models with opposite objectives, utilizing a generator to produce synthetic data and a discriminator to classify it. This approach is particularly effective in training models on unbalanced datasets, where it can enhance performance and provide robustness against data perturbations. We demonstrate the efficacy of AAT in fraud detection tasks using both synthetic and imbalanced real-world datasets, highlighting its superiority over traditional GAN-based training methods. Furthermore, we show that AAT can produce high-quality data augmentation, leading to improved generalization and robustness against adversarial attacks. This document provides a comprehensive overview of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section calculation in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, including various background and signal processes within the ATLAS detector. The analysis focuses on events with one b-tagged jet, either originating from the $t\bar{t}$ signal or the $W$+jets background. A novel method is presented that allows for the simultaneous estimation of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section and the $W$-jet scale factor. By combining data collected from 2015, 2016, and part of 2017, the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section is measured at 137.0 pb, accompanied by an uncertainty of 0.4 pb. This analysis also explores the $W$-jet scale factor using a combination of data-driven methods and theoretical predictions. Additionally, differential cross-sections are presented for the $t\bar{t}$ production process, including the $W$-jet scale factor, as a function of various kinematic variables. The results are compared to the predictions from the Monte Carlo generator MC@NLO with parton-shower method and the next-to-leading-order predictions from the POWHEG box resummation method. All presented cross-sections are also provided with theoretical and experimental systematic uncertainties. This analysis also includes a comparison of the $W$-jet scale factor obtained from the two methods with that obtained from the ATLAS measurement of the $W$ boson mass. Furthermore, the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section is also calculated for various kinematic variables, including the transverse momentum of the top quark and the b-tagged jet. Lastly, the $t\bar{t}$ production in association with additional heavy-flavour jets is discussed. This analysis is based on a dataset collected with the ATLAS detector at the LHC operating at 13 TeV centre-of-mass energy, corresponding to 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. This dataset is used to measure the cross-sections for the $t\bar{t}$ production in association with additional heavy-flavour jets. By combining data collected from 2015 and 2016, the cross-section is measured at 0.25 pb with an uncertainty of 0.06 pb. This analysis also explores the $W$-jet scale factor using a combination of data-driven methods and theoretical predictions. Link prediction, a crucial component of information networks, has been extensively researched over the years. The majority of existing methods fail to capture the intricate dynamics of time-evolving graphs, leading to suboptimal performance in long-term forecasting. In an effort to bridge this gap, researchers have developed novel methods that incorporate time-aware representations and utilize short-term forecasts as a foundation for long-term predictions. However, these approaches often neglect to incorporate the contextual and semantic connections between nodes, which are vital factors influencing link evolution. To address this limitation, a new framework, called Generalized Connection Learning with Semantic Correlation Recognition (GCL-SCR), has been proposed. The GCL-SCR framework is capable of capturing both semantic and temporal connections between nodes, enabling it to predict links based on meaningful correlations. Furthermore, a novel loss function has been designed to optimize the learning process by incorporating a fairness constraint, ensuring that similar nodes exhibit similar meaningful correlations. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of GCL-SCR in accurately predicting links across diverse domains, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper proposes a novel approach, LEAP, that harnesses the capabilities of edge computing to deliver a secure and efficient LBS platform. Leveraging edge servers, LEAP ensures user location privacy by only processing and relaying information to service providers via edge servers, thus preventing any direct contact between users and providers. Additionally, LEAP optimizes data transmission by employing a distance-based method to determine the nearest edge server to the service provider. An extensive evaluation of LEAP using real-world datasets reveals its superiority over existing protocols, boasting a significant reduction of up to 66.7% in communication costs. Comparisons with other protocols also show that LEAP achieves substantial performance improvements. including the classical L-series Li_k(z_1,...,z_k) for k>0 and complex z_i in C. 
This algebra incorporates L-functions L_k(z_1,...,z_k; s), allowing for the 
representation of motivic functions on the complex projective space. 
Motivic functions are defined as functions that extend the meromorphic 
continuation of L_k(z_1,...,z_k; s) across the entire s-plane. 
We demonstrate the existence of a Hopf algebra that represents analytic 1-forms 
on the complex projective space, thereby providing a tool for analyzing 
motivic functions through a cohomological approach. 
We establish that the Hopf algebra's co-invariants yield the meromorphic 
continuation of L_k(z_1,...,z_k; s) for all k>0. 
This work extends the research of a 2019 paper by the same authors, 
which investigated the case of L_2(z_1,z_2; s) and L_3(z_1,z_2,z_3; s). 
A 2020 paper by the authors in collaboration with A. G\'eh\`ermiston explored 
the case of L_2(z_1,z_2; z_3).

meromorphic continuation of the product L_2(z_1,z_2; s_1,s_2) and L_2(z_3,z_4; s_3,s_4; s_1,s_2).

Recent research has highlighted the severe vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks that alter model behavior. Existing methods for introducing neural backdoors through adversarial attacks, however, require significant modifications to the input data and are prone to detection. To address this issue, we investigate a more stealthy approach: manipulating a model's weights directly to introduce a backdoor signal. We examine the solvability of Dirichlet problems for a broad class of non-autonomous linear parabolic equations. The equations are defined in a region with a bounded boundary and an unbounded exterior. The problems are formulated in weighted Sobolev spaces that adhere to the boundary conditions. A key finding is a trace theorem characterizing the relationship between weighted Sobolev spaces on the interior versus the boundary. Building on this foundation, we demonstrate the non-existence of non-trivial solutions for a specific class of Dirichlet problems. Furthermore, we establish the solvability of Robin problems under a combination of two conditions: (i) the Robin parameter is sufficiently negative and (ii) the boundary of the domain exhibits sufficient regularity. The Dirichlet-Neumann problems, however, are found to be inherently ill-posed. To address this issue, we introduce a regularization method that relies on the Robin problem and gradually approaches a Dirichlet boundary condition through a sequence of adjustable parameters. The method is shown to converge in a manner consistent with the rate of convergence of the underlying iterative algorithm. Theoretical findings are supplemented by a series of numerical experiments. The numerical simulations, in turn, are validated against the theoretical predictions. Ultimately, the application of this regularization method is illustrated by considering a specific example involving the one-dimensional heat equation. This work generalizes earlier research on the same topic, originally published in the paper "Non-unique and Ill-posed Dirichlet-Neumann problems in parabolic PDEs" by the same authors in the journal Mathematics of Computation in 2020. In the field of autonomous driving, it is crucial to develop policies that are
sociably acceptable, taking into account the behavior of other road users and
prioritize safety.  However, the policies must also be adaptable to various
scenarios and individual driving styles. To address this challenge, we propose a
novel approach that utilizes a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning
method. This method enables the creation of socially acceptable driving
behaviors while allowing for individual driving styles to be factored in. Our
approach is tested in a diverse setting that includes a mix of road users and
customizable driving styles.  Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric
that assesses the degree of individual driving style influence on the overall
road behavior. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully
creates policies that are both adaptable and sociably acceptable, and these
policies can be easily fine-tuned to fit individual driving styles. Moreover, our
approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both driving style influence
and road safety. The code for our method is available on GitHub. https://github.com/autolab-qmuc/human-empowered-social-guidance.

This is modeled using the quantum Brownian motion equation, where measurement affects the system's interaction with a bath of harmonic oscillators. As a first-order approximation, measurement's effect on the system's wavefunction is modified to include a phase shift proportional to the system's momentum and wavefunction overlap. When measurement is repeated at a rate close to the bath's relaxation rate, it's found that measurement can either prevent (Zeno effect) or induce (anti-Zeno effect) changes in the system's state, leading to faster or slower evolution. This behavior is observed in two scenarios: the system evolving in a harmonic trap, and being driven by a time-dependent force. In the first case, measurement can prevent the system from falling into a potential well, and in the second case, it can speed up or slow down the system's quantum state collapse. This behavior is attributed to measurement-induced fluctuations in the system's momentum. Interestingly, measurement that is too frequent can prevent the system from making a transition to a stable state, but too frequent measurement can eventually force the system into a stable state. This behavior is attributed to the interplay between the measurement-induced fluctuations and the system's dissipation. The rapid advancements in targeted therapy have accelerated cancer progression by driving the growth of genetically diverse cancer cells. To effectively combat this, it is crucial to understand the complex interactions between cancer cells and their microenvironment. However, due to the high computational costs associated with modeling these interactions, existing models are often limited and simplified. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a novel approach called OG-SPACE, a stochastic simulation framework that efficiently models cancer evolution in a detailed, geospatial environment. OG-SPACE builds on the existing Space-Explicit Random Discrete Event simulation (SPACERD) framework and incorporates two key features: the Organoid Growth (OG) model and the Spatial Proximity (SP) algorithm. The OG model captures the dynamic growth of tumor spheroids, while the SP algorithm tracks the proximity of cells to their surroundings, enabling the simulation of interactions between cells and their microenvironment. To demonstrate the capabilities of OG-SPACE, researchers applied it to a real-world scenario involving a patient with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The results showed that the simulated tumor evolved into distinct clones, characterized by genetic mutations, such as KRAS and TP53. Furthermore, simulations revealed that the microenvironment played a crucial role in shaping the tumor's genetic diversity, highlighting the importance of modeling these interactions to develop effective cancer treatments. The OG-SPACE framework is now available to the scientific community and can be used to study cancer progression and inform the development of more effective therapies. learning modules, to effectively leverage both supervised and semi-supervised
data. Initially, we utilize a supervised approach to generate high-quality
features, which are then used in a semi-supervised framework to further refine
them. FlexMatch employs a curriculum learning strategy to adjust its difficulty
levels by implementing a pseudo-tag thresholding mechanism. This technique
demonstrates significant improvements in performance, achieving the state-of-the-art
result of 71.0\% on ImageNet-1K with a multi-step fine-tuning pipeline. 
Additionally, we show that FlexMatch surpasses the performance of DeCoRL, another
state-of-the-art method, by a notable margin, achieving a 5.0\% gain in the same
benchmark. Moreover, we observe that FlexMatch outperforms other leading methods,
such as DeCoRL, FixMatch, and UDA, in the ImageNet validation set, achieving a
71.0\% top-1 accuracy. FlexMatch also achieves the best results in ImageNet-Sketch
at 69.9\% top-1 accuracy. FlexMatch is implemented in MMDetection and its source
code is available on GitHub. The associated experiment scripts are also provided.

A novel non-convex, non-global energy function is introduced to detect visual salience by identifying important regions within an image that are relevant to the overall scene. Diverging from conventional global energy approaches that minimize distractions to capture global meaning, the non-global energy here encourages the recognition of both local and global significance. This non-global energy function is comprised of two key components: a local term that aims to identify coherent, salient features and a global term that aims to integrate these features into the overall scene. Utilizing non-convex constraints, the local term promotes the recognition of diverse and meaningful features, whereas the global term ensures their integration. This integration is achieved by leveraging the principles of convex analysis, which enables the derivation of an efficient algorithm for its solution. Through rigorous testing on a diverse set of 50 images, the non-global energy function is demonstrated to outperform state-of-the-art methods in salience detection, particularly in recognizing intricate, scene-specific features. Additionally, the results of combining this method with other approaches, such as multi-scale saliency integration and deep neural networks, are found to be highly effective in enhancing visual saliency detection. However, the effectiveness of these methods depends on the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$, with significant differences arising when the spectrum changes. This study focuses on the geometric convergence characteristics of several preconditioned solvers and examines how the preconditioning matrix influences this process. By leveraging the gradient descent method, the convergence properties of these solvers can be comprehensively analyzed. Notably, the research reveals that the preconditioning matrix affects the preconditioned conjugate gradient method's convergence rate, particularly for the Chebyshev method, which fails to achieve fast convergence when the spectrum is clustered around zero. This study provides an innovative approach to understanding the behavior of preconditioned eigenvalue solvers. The associated code is publicly available. In intelligent building monitoring systems, various cameras are installed both indoors and outdoors to ensure security and efficient operation of the building. However, verifying the identity of individuals entering buildings via cameras poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel solution called the motion-sensitive pseudo siamese network (MPSN) that leverages motion data from camera systems to identify individuals. By analyzing motion data, MPSN generates a motion-sensitive feature, which is then used to train a deep neural network (DNN) for identification purposes. To further enhance the identification process, MPSN also extracts facial features from images and trains a separate DNN to match these features. Our solution's effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive experiments conducted using two large-scale indoor video datasets. Our MPSN model achieved an impressive identification accuracy of 99.67% and 99.74% on the first dataset, and 99.56% and 99.64% on the second dataset, respectively. Moreover, our MPSN model's ability to identify individuals based solely on motion data and minimal facial images is demonstrated. Details of the experimental settings, datasets, and code for reproducing our results can be found on our GitHub repository. This is the first study to utilize motion data for identification purposes in indoor video head identification. Given a sentence describing a person's pose, TIPS uses a single neural model to analyze the sentence and produce a detailed 2D body outline, which is then enhanced with realistic skin texture and color. Through extensive testing on a large, real-world dataset, TIPS achieves highly realistic results that accurately capture the face and overall pose, while also enabling a range of creative applications. Our research sets a new benchmark for generating custom human images from text descriptions and opens up exciting possibilities for future visual applications. By adopting the complete-image warping strategy from the foundational work of Chen et al., and building upon the differentiable operator abstraction of the RAFT model, we improve the representation capabilities of the network. A novel approach to self-training involves generating pseudo-labels for subsequent time steps based on the predicted flow field from the preceding step. This self-supervised method enables the network to refine its predictions and ultimately achieve superior performance, as demonstrated by a significant 25% reduction in mean absolute error on the Flying Chairs benchmark compared to the original RAFT network. Furthermore, SMURF surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, as well as outperforms competing approaches that leverage multi-frame information, while operating without the need for any supervision. A novel approach is presented for creating high-quality density maps from noisy data, which is an integral component of many fields including robotics, medical imaging, and computer vision. Our method leverages a trans-dimensional MCMC sampler to identify the most effective Gaussian mixture model for a given dataset, thereby producing an optimal density map. In contrast to existing density-mapping techniques, this approach does not rely on smoothing or regularization. In addition to theoretical justifications, our method's performance is validated through experiments using synthetic datasets. A comprehensive comparison with established density-mapping methods demonstrates that our approach yields superior results when using sparse, noisy data. Notably, our method does not require the user to specify the number of underlying densities or sampling resolution. Instead, this information is inferred automatically through trans-dimensional inference, thereby eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning. In a robotic application, our method successfully identifies the most likely path of a robot within a complex environment. In this context, it is demonstrated that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness to noise. A two-dimensional, active-inert fluid interaction model has been developed, grounded in a generalized logistic equation with sensitivity-dependent chemotactic sensitivity that depends on both chemokines and population density. By analyzing this model under initial condition bounds and assuming specific parameter values, we have demonstrated that population density and chemokines converge to global solutions of a lower-dimensional model within a specific functional space. This lower-dimensional model is characterized by an advective-diffusive structure for chemokines and a logistic equation with sensitivity-dependent chemotactic drift for the population density. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations. This research builds upon previous studies exploring similar models in a two-dimensional space. Our results have implications for the design of self-regulating systems in biology, and our work may shed light on understanding cancer progression. Fault-tolerant computing technology is crucial in areas such as aerospace, defense, healthcare, and autonomous vehicles. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown that neuroevolutionary methods can be used to design fault-tolerant systems. This research introduces a novel approach to the piecewise steady image restoration problem, framed as a minimax optimization issue that incorporates a dual stage continuous domain regularization framework. By leveraging a variational model with adjustable parameters, it effectively addresses the diverse characteristics of various image segments. A dual stage approach utilizes a binary variable to partition the image into distinct segments, where each part is then refined through a variational model with tailored parameters. The dual stage regularization framework is composed of two primary components: a binary variable update module and a segment-specific model update module. The former updates the binary variable by minimizing a surrogate continuity error, while the latter refines each segment using a variational model with adaptive parameters. This paper presents two variants of the dual stage continuous domain regularization module, one relying on a primal-dual dynamic method and the other using a proximal block coordinate descent algorithm. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of the dual stage continuous domain regularization algorithm, while experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over existing state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real-world image data. A novel IoT management approach, Self-Managed IoT, has been proposed, enabling users to fully control their personal computation tasks. In Self-Managed IoT, users are empowered to decide where to run tasks, either on their devices or within a cloud, based on their preferences. A key component of this system is a personal management entity, called PME, which assists users in offloading tasks, monitors resource usage, and ensures users remain fully knowledgeable about their data. In contrast to existing offloading systems, Self-Managed IoT is the first to integrate user authority with task offloading, offering a more comprehensive and user-centric solution. Through experiments and simulations, the system's capabilities have been validated, with results showing significant improvements over current practices. Specifically, Self-Managed IoT is expected to enhance user productivity by 2.5 times and reduce energy consumption by 3.5 times compared to traditional device-based approaches. Moreover, the system's task offloading efficiency is significantly higher than existing offloading systems, with performance enhancements of 2.5 times and 1.5 times respectively. Real-world experiments have also demonstrated the practical feasibility of Self-Managed IoT, with promising outcomes on both Android and Linux platforms. The goal of Visual Inquiry Answering (VIA) involves an interactive process, where a model responds to queries based on an image. Current models primarily excel within their trained datasets but struggle when applied to unfamiliar domains. To address this limitation, we introduce Enhanced RAMEN, an improved RAMEN framework that enables it to generate more accurate and relevant responses to queries. We achieve this by developing a cross-attention based Visual Question Answering (VQA) model that leverages multimodal information, including text data. This model utilizes the text information to effectively answer queries and identify the most relevant region within the image. We also introduce a new dataset called GPT, which is a subset of the GQA dataset and serves as a test case for evaluating domain generalization in VIA. Experiments conducted using the GPT and GPT-10 datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model compared to existing RAMEN and T5 models. The source code for Enhanced RAMEN is publicly available on the GitHub repository.

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance the performance of model-based Reinforcement Learning by integrating the strengths of both Model Predictive Control and value function estimation methods. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that the optimal solution to a temporary problem solved by Model Predictive Control actually serves as a reliable guideline for constructing an informed value function. Furthermore, we show that using Model Predictive Control can be viewed as an efficient method for improving value function estimation, which in turn enables faster and more accurate decision-making. Based on these findings, we propose a hybrid RL algorithm that combines both Model Predictive Control and value function estimation techniques. Through extensive testing on various complex environments, including high-dimensional tasks and continuous control scenarios, we successfully validate the enhanced performance of our proposed approach. Specifically, our results reveal significant improvements in terms of both sample efficiency and final performance, which outshine existing model-based and value function estimation methods in substantial margins. For instance, our approach excels in sample efficiency by up to 40 times and final performance by up to 20% compared to the most effective baseline in the context of continuous control. Moreover, our approach is also capable of achieving superior performance in the challenging domain of high-dimensional images, where state-space dimensions are in the order of thousands. Ultimately, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between model-based and model-free RL methods, which may pave the way for future breakthroughs in RL research. We investigate how many disks two randomly positioned and sized points can intersect on average, given a certain number of points. To tackle this problem, we present upper and lower bounds for the number of intersections. Upper bounds are achieved by assuming the points are separated by the sum of their radii plus a small gap, under the condition that the points are randomly distributed on a disk. To get lower bounds, we examine the arrangement of points that maximizes the number of intersections, considering cases where the points touch each other and those separated by a certain distance, either a fixed radius or one growing with the number of points. Our findings indicate that the actual number of intersections lies between the calculated upper and lower limits. However, the exact number of intersections remains unknown for all cases except when the number of points is equal to or less than four. In conversational AI, dialogue systems are being employed in various real-world applications, encompassing customer service, technical support, and educational settings. However, existing research primarily focuses on developing these systems for specific, broad goals such as customer service or information search. This paper proposes that more flexible and personalized approaches are required to effectively support diverse user objectives within a particular context. Specifically, we advocate for dialogue systems that can adapt to individual users' distinct identities, preferences, and knowledge backgrounds. Moreover, we highlight the significance of grounding these personal characteristics and associated assumptions in order to implement tailored conversational AI effectively. This requires a more nuanced understanding of the user's identity and can be achieved through the use of natural language processing and information extraction methods. Ultimately, we contend that the integration of personalized, identity-based dialogue systems can lead to the development of more versatile, adaptable, and effective conversational agents. Moreover, we suggest that the ability to understand and accommodate individual differences could also contribute to the creation of more inclusive AI products. This perspective piece aims to stimulate further research in this area, particularly in the areas of education, mental health, and human-computer interaction. Ultimately, we hope to encourage researchers to explore the practical applications of these ideas and contribute to the advancement of more personalized and effective conversational AI systems.

Our findings are supported by experiments using various deep learning models and optimization methods. The proposed approach is based on a hierarchical attribute model, where the top-level attributes serve as a compact representation and lower-level attributes provide more detailed semantic information. We evaluate our approach on a large dataset of images from the ImageNet-1K and MS-COCO datasets, showing that it can learn a compact set of attributes that effectively capture a wide range of variations.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be used to generate novel attributes by combining existing ones in a meta-learning framework, which we term MetaKernel. This behavior, known as satisficing, has been observed in humans and other agents, such as autonomous vehicles, which may default to safe modes when they encounter unpredictable situations. This decision-making approach, which balances exploration and exploitation, may provide a solution to the challenge of learning in uncertain environments. This paper explores the properties of satisficing agents in a multi-agent setting and examines how their decision-making affects the dynamics of their interactions. We show that the interaction between different strategies leads to the emergence of new strategies that are more resilient to uncertainty than the individual agents' approaches. For a given algebraic group G and a given finite-dimensional irreducible representation V, we characterize the orbits resulting from G's action on algebraic varieties of the form G\times_V V. Specifically, we focus on the case where V is a three-dimensional special representation of GL_3, yielding quadruple projective spaces. Through the application of monoidal sheaf-ification, we divide these orbits into distinct G-orbits, each corresponding to a unique orbit closure. We further identify the structure of these orbit closures as GL_3\times GL_3-modular irreducible representations, detailing their properties. Most notably, we establish that orbit closures corresponding to non-isomorphic orbits never coincide, while we also provide a detailed analysis of the exceptional isomorphisms observed. Notably, we also validate the long-standing conjecture of Van Oystaeyen, demonstrating that orbit closures corresponding to non-equivalent orbits never coincide, except in the case of the exceptional isomorphisms. This work also provides a thorough classification of the orbits resulting from G = GL_2 and V = V_2, offering new insights into the structure of GL_2-modular irreducible representations. Finally, we explore potential areas for further investigation. This research draws heavily from the author's previous work on characterizing GL_2-orbits on projective varieties. For the benefit of readers, we include a brief review of the necessary concepts and results. In modern networks, traffic management through Multi-Protocol Label Switching is crucial for efficient communication. However, its opaque nature complicates the monitoring process. Research has shown that by strategically sending packets through the network core, the sender's identity can be revealed, making it essential to conceal this information. Our study explores this issue, particularly in data centers, where we discovered that implementing countermeasures is often as easy as disabling fast-forwarding, forwarding traffic to non-existent or inactive destinations, and using the shortest path. Our results indicate that, in reality, most networks do not employ countermeasures, thereby allowing us to map the inner workings of MPLS networks and access sensitive data, even from outside the network. Open information extraction, which extracts individual facts from large text collections, has been a significant challenge in the field of information extraction. While existing open extraction systems, such as Matcher-A act as general language processing tools, they often struggle to maintain context when extracting facts from complex sentences. To address this issue, we introduce Graphene, a novel open extraction system that utilizes a graph-based structure to incorporate contextual information during the fact extraction process. By incorporating a graph-based approach, Graphene is able to capture the nuances of complex sentences and related concepts, which in turn leads to improved accuracy in and coverage of open extraction. Our evaluation of Graphene on publicly available datasets reveals a notable improvement in both accuracy and coverage compared to existing state-of-the-art systems, with a significant gain in coverage. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of Graphene by showcasing its ability to extract complex multi-participant events from a large corpus of news articles. Overall, our results suggest that Graphene has the potential to revolutionize the field of open extraction, allowing for the extraction of a more comprehensive set of facts from large text collections. In response to this issue, we propose a new definition of attribution that focuses on the stability of a model's conclusions over time, rather than the attribution of a feature to those conclusions. We also introduce a new metric to measure the stability of attribution, and we conduct a comprehensive study to evaluate the impact of this new definition on the interpretation of model outcomes.  The results of our study suggest that the new definition of attribution provides more reliable and more stable explanations for model decisions. Code smells are perceived by the software community as indicators of poor system design and reflective of underlying technical issues. They are seen as contributing factors to the emergence of more severe software maintenance problems. Research has focused on identifying the removal of code smells as a key challenge in software maintenance. However, prior studies have not provided a comprehensive overview of the current state of research in this area. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic analysis of 145 papers from 2012 to 2022, examining 15 key aspects of code smells detection. Our analysis revealed that recent research is increasingly focused on machine learning approaches, particularly when combined with software metrics. Notably, the study found that research in code smells detection is becoming more widespread but less concentrated in specific areas. We also identified a lack of standardization in code smells detection tools, which often require manual configuration. Our results provide a valuable framework for future research in code smells detection. Our code and data sets are publicly available, allowing others to build upon our findings. This study examines how the introduction of opposing views within a group of like-minded individuals affects the formation of public sentiments. We investigate how exposure to opposing views, in an environment where the dissemination of negative information incurs costs, influences the creation of public sentiments. We analyze the effects of this scenario in both homogeneous and heterogeneous social networks, discovering that the introduction of opposing views within a group can lead to a'stack effect,' where initial exposure to opposing views before aligned views has the most significant impact. We also find that the introduction of opposing views within a group can lead to a 'backfire effect,' where exposure to opposing views results in increased alignment of opinions. Furthermore, we find that varying levels of exposure to opposing views within a group can lead to a 'threshold effect,' where increased exposure to opposing views has the most significant impact initially but has little to no effect when exposed excessively. Lastly, we find that introducing random connections within a group can lead to a 'network effect,' where exposure to opposing views has the most significant impact through random connections rather than direct ones. The physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach has gained significant attention for solving a broad range of coupled ordinary differential equation (ODE) problems. However, the assessment of PINN solutions is often hindered by the introduction of overly complex neural network architectures that provide overly confident yet inaccurate predictions. We propose a novel approach that incorporates a trainable threshold for determining the accuracy of PINN predictions, and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments in both spatially distributed and time-dependent ODE problems. Our results show that this method effectively identifies overconfident predictions and achieves comparable or superior performance compared to existing evaluation techniques. Furthermore, we highlight the potential limitations of this method and offer potential avenues for future research in this area. The code and datasets used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. The findings of this work are expected to facilitate the development of more reliable and accurate PINN solutions for solving ODE problems. Video communication plays a vital role in our daily lives, but transmitting high-quality videos at low bandwidth is a significant challenge. Although recent advancements in neural compression have made significant progress, current methods fall short in balancing compression efficiency and robustness. To address this issue, we present Gemino, a pioneering framework that effectively and reliably compresses videos. By integrating a novel two-stage quantization method and a robust deblocking mechanism, Gemino significantly improves both the quality and resilience of compressed videos, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 2.39 dB and 2.73 dB, respectively. Furthermore, Gemino's results are found to be highly consistent across various video resolutions and quality assessments. Moreover, its end-to-end optimization enables it to achieve optimal performance with minimal computational overhead. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate the substantial benefits of using Gemino, showcasing a 38.7% reduction in bandwidth usage with only a 1.9% increase in video quality. Overall, Gemino presents a groundbreaking approach to neural compression, enabling the effective and resilient transmission of high-quality videos over low-bandwidth channels. Its open-source implementation is available on GitHub for further research and development. Additionally, our research includes extensive experiments that demonstrate the robustness of compressed video transmission, revealing a 50.8% reduction in error rates and a 60.2% decrease in packet errors for a given transmission error rate. These findings underscore the significance of developing robust neural compression methods for reliable video transmission. Finally, our research also explores the application of Gemino in real-world video communication, revealing its potential to significantly enhance the quality of live video transmission, particularly in 5G networks. Specifically, Gemino's application in live video transmission enables the delivery of high-quality videos with a bandwidth reduction of up to 35.6% and an error rate decrease of 53.6%. These results highlight the potential of Gemino to revolutionize live video communication systems. The field of open-set identification addresses the challenge of recognizing objects that fall outside a predefined reference set. Specifically, we utilize a similarity metric to measure the distance between test samples and their nearest in-distribution neighbors, generating a distribution of similarity scores in the process. The distribution is then processed using a neural network to obtain an out-of-scope probability, which is ultimately used to identify samples that fall outside the reference set. To enhance the model's generalizability, we employ a novel training objective that involves generating similarity scores for images that do not exist in the reference set. This approach allows us to effectively utilize the available unlabeled data and significantly improve the model's performance. The proposed method, which is referred to as augmentation-driven similarity learning, has been successfully evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
